plainDefinition: Software that learns what a person's voice sounds like from recordings, then generates new speech in that voice saying things the person may never have said.
whyItMatters: A cloned voice can record a new radio ad in minutes, or it can put words in a real person's mouth. The technology is identical; the disclosure and consent are what separate a tool from a deception.
howToSpot: Listen for flat emotional range, odd pacing around names and numbers, and breathing that never varies. When a clip sounds slightly too clean for a phone line or a rally, ask where the original recording came from.

plainDefinition: A video or audio clip manipulated by AI so a real person appears to say or do something they never said or did.
whyItMatters: Deepfakes target the basic trust voters place in their own eyes and ears. Even a clumsy fake can spread for hours before a correction catches up, and the correction never travels as far as the fake.
howToSpot: Check the edges: hairlines, glasses, teeth, and hands glitch first. Look for mismatched lighting between face and background, and search for the original clip. If a moment seems perfectly designed to outrage you, verify before you share.

plainDefinition: Any image, audio, or video created or substantially altered by AI rather than captured by a camera or microphone.
whyItMatters: Synthetic media is not automatically deceptive. An animated explainer is synthetic; so is a fabricated scandal clip. What matters is whether the audience is told what was created and what was captured.
howToSpot: Look for disclosure labels, check whether the scene could physically have been filmed, and notice textures: skin, water, text, and crowds are hard for AI to render consistently.

plainDefinition: The plain-language line between footage recorded from real life (captured) and imagery generated or heavily altered by software (created).
whyItMatters: This distinction is the foundation of honest AI disclosure. Voters do not need a technical breakdown; they need to know which parts of what they are watching happened in front of a camera.
howToSpot: Well-labeled ads increasingly say it outright: "Real event footage" or "AI-generated imagery." When a label is missing, ask whether the moment on screen could have been filmed at all.

plainDefinition: AI systems that produce new content, such as text, images, audio, or video, from a prompt, based on patterns learned from enormous amounts of existing material.
whyItMatters: Generative AI collapses the cost of producing campaign content of every kind. That levels the field for small campaigns and simultaneously lowers the cost of producing misleading content at scale.
howToSpot: You usually cannot spot it from the output alone anymore. Look for disclosure, provenance information, and the publisher's track record instead of trusting your eyes.

plainDefinition: A computer-generated voice reading a script, used in place of a human voiceover artist.
whyItMatters: AI narration makes professional-sounding video affordable for campaigns that could never hire studio talent. Used with disclosure, it is a production tool; used to imitate a specific real person, it becomes voice cloning.
howToSpot: Generic AI narration sounds polished but placeless: no regional accent, perfectly even emphasis. Many honest ads now disclose it directly in the credits or the spoken track.

plainDefinition: Using AI to help draft, tighten, or restructure the words of an ad, speech, or post, with a human deciding what is actually said.
whyItMatters: This is one of the most common and least alarming campaign uses of AI: a drafting partner. The judgment calls, the claims, and the promises still belong to the humans who approve the script.
howToSpot: You generally cannot, and that is fine. Watch for whether claims are accurate and whether a real person stands behind them, not whether software helped with the wording.

plainDefinition: Splitting an audience into very narrow slices, sometimes down to a few hundred people, and showing each slice a message tailored specifically to it.
whyItMatters: Tailored messages can be relevance or manipulation. When every slice sees a different promise and nobody sees the whole picture, public accountability gets harder.
howToSpot: Use the platform's own ad transparency tools: "Why am I seeing this ad?" and public ad libraries show how narrowly an ad was aimed and by whom.

plainDefinition: A targeting technique where a platform finds new people who statistically resemble a group you already know, such as your existing donors.
whyItMatters: Lookalikes are how small donor lists become large fundraising programs. They also mean you can be targeted because of what strangers who resemble you have done, not anything you chose.
howToSpot: If you donated to one cause and suddenly see appeals from many similar ones, a lookalike model probably found you. Platform ad-transparency panels sometimes say an advertiser used a customer list to reach you.

plainDefinition: The public record of registered voters, including party registration and election turnout history, that campaigns license, clean, and enrich with additional data.
whyItMatters: The voter file is the backbone of almost every campaign's outreach on every side. Knowing it exists explains a lot: campaigns know whether you vote, and they spend accordingly.
howToSpot: You cannot see the file itself, but mail addressed to the registered voter in your household, or door-knockers with your first name on a clipboard, are the voter file at work.

plainDefinition: Statistical scoring that predicts things about individual voters, such as how likely they are to turn out, persuadable they are, or care about a given issue.
whyItMatters: Models decide who gets a knock, a call, or an ad, and who gets ignored. A wrong score is invisible to the person it mislabels, and being ignored by campaigns is a real civic cost.
howToSpot: You mostly experience it as absence or intensity: a flood of attention in a close race if you score as persuadable, silence if you do not.

plainDefinition: Sending two or more versions of the same message to samples of an audience, measuring which performs better, and then sending the winner to everyone else.
whyItMatters: Testing is standard practice in fundraising email and ads across the spectrum. It quietly optimizes for what makes people click and give, which is often urgency and alarm, not accuracy.
howToSpot: Compare notes with a friend on the same list: different subject lines for the same email are a test in progress. So are near-identical ads with one changed sentence.

plainDefinition: Advertising bought and placed by software in automated auctions, deciding in milliseconds which ad you see on which page or app.
whyItMatters: Most digital political advertising moves through these automated markets. Speed and scale make oversight hard: an ad can reach millions before a human reviewer ever looks at it.
howToSpot: Political ads that follow you across unrelated websites and apps are programmatic. Ad libraries and the small "i" or "AdChoices" icons show who paid.

plainDefinition: The software that decides which posts, videos, or channels a platform suggests to you next, optimizing for whatever keeps you engaged.
whyItMatters: Campaign content lives or dies by these systems, so campaigns produce what the algorithm rewards. That shapes political speech itself, usually toward the emotional and the brief.
howToSpot: Notice when you never searched for something but keep seeing more of it. "Suggested for you" and autoplay queues are the algorithm speaking.

plainDefinition: A social media timeline ordered by predicted engagement rather than by time, so software chooses what you see first and what you never see at all.
whyItMatters: Two neighbors following identical accounts can see entirely different campaigns. The feed is each voter's private front page, assembled by prediction, and no editor is accountable for it.
howToSpot: If posts appear out of chronological order, or a friend saw an announcement you never did, you are in an algorithmic feed. Many platforms hide a "latest" or "following" toggle that shows the difference.

plainDefinition: Software that sends texts, emails, or social replies to large lists on a schedule or trigger, with message content queued up in advance by the campaign.
whyItMatters: Automation is how a five-person campaign talks to fifty thousand voters. It also means the "personal" message you received was personal for thousands of people at once.
howToSpot: Instant replies at odd hours, your first name inserted a little too mechanically, and texts from a rotating set of unfamiliar numbers are hallmarks of automation.

plainDefinition: A program that holds text conversations automatically, answering questions or making an ask, sometimes while presenting itself like a human volunteer.
whyItMatters: A well-labeled chatbot answering polling-place questions at 2am is a genuine service. The ethical line is impersonation: voters deserve to know when they are talking to software.
howToSpot: Instant, perfectly typed responses to anything you send, graceful dodges of unexpected questions, and a suspicious eagerness to return to the script suggest a bot. Honest ones say so when asked directly.

plainDefinition: Software that reads large volumes of posts, comments, or replies and estimates how people feel about a candidate or issue.
whyItMatters: Campaigns use it as a real-time focus group. It is cheap and fast, but it reads the loudest voices online, which are not the same as the electorate.
howToSpot: You will not see it directly. Its fingerprints are rapid message changes after an online storm, or talking points that answer yesterday's trending complaint.

plainDefinition: The on-screen or spoken notice telling the audience that AI was used to create or alter part of what they are seeing or hearing.
whyItMatters: Labels are the difference between a production technique and a deception. A meaningful label says what was AI-made and what was real, not just a generic stamp in tiny print.
howToSpot: Look for wording in the ad itself: a lower-third line, a spoken sentence, or an end card. Several states require specific wording for political ads that use synthetic media.

plainDefinition: The verifiable history of a piece of media: where it came from, when it was captured or created, and what has been done to it since.
whyItMatters: When anything can be faked, proving where real footage came from becomes as important as spotting fakes. Provenance standards let a photo or video carry its receipts with it.
howToSpot: Look for content-credential icons or "about this image" panels on platforms that support them, showing capture device, edit history, and signing organization.

plainDefinition: Software that learns when each person on a list is most likely to open a message and schedules delivery for that moment, individually.
whyItMatters: It is a small, everyday example of AI in campaigns: no content changes at all, just timing. Multiplied across millions of messages, it measurably moves fundraising and turnout numbers.
howToSpot: Campaign email that reliably lands right when you tend to check your phone is not a coincidence; it is a model that learned your habits from your open history.
